tasks.task_description: Task 1: develop a mathematical model that explains the listing price of each sailboat in the supplied spreadsheet, using any useful predictors, identifying all data sources, and discussing the precision of the estimate for each sailboat variant's price.
tasks.task_analysis: Approach: a hedonic (log-linear) regression is the standard and sound choice for used-asset prices -- it turns multiplicative price drivers into additive coefficients, keeps all fitted prices positive, and makes each coefficient a directly interpretable price ratio, which is exactly what a broker needs.  We model on the log of price.  Predictors: length, age (2020-year), geographic region, hull type, and a make-variant family effect that carries the design/quality differences between models (the single largest source of variation; two 45-ft boats of the same age can differ 2-3x purely by model).  Data cleaning (stated in the scope note): 3491 rows (2346 monohull, 1145 catamaran); year normalised (catamaran years were stored as '\xa0'-prefixed strings); make/variant whitespace stripped (103 makes, 34 variants had trailing spaces); 3 monohull rows with a blank country left null and unused; 1210 numeric variant labels kept as string model designations.  No missing prices; all prices >0; years 2005-2019; lengths 36-56 ft.  Method is OLS, validated by R2 and by the within-family residual structure.  Assumptions: listing price is the observable proxy for value (not final sale price, so it carries seller markup and is a noisy but unbiased indicator of market price); the December-2020 snapshot is a cross-section so age = 2020-year; region and hull effects are treated as multiplicative on price; the 580 families are assumed internally homogeneous enough for a single family effect.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Log-linear hedonic model.  Dependent variable ln(Price) (Price in USD), all predictors enter on the log/linear scale so coefficients read as price ratios.
Full (within-family) specification:
  ln Price = b0 + b_L*L + b_age*Age + b_USA*I(USA) + b_Carib*I(Caribbean)
             + sum_f gamma_f * I(make-variant family == f)      [579 family dummies, 1 baseline]
where L = length (ft), Age = 2020 - Year, region Europe is the baseline.  The 580 make-variant families (82 makes) carry design/quality differences; the region dummies are then the *pure* geographic effect with the identical boat held fixed.  Fit by OLS on 3491 rows -> R2 = 0.928.  Fitted: b_L = 0.00275 (nearly 0 within a family, because length is almost constant inside a family), b_age = -0.04944 (-4.82%/yr), b_USA = 0.1769, b_Carib = -0.0534.
Cross-family (pooled) specification, used for the length and hull effects that the family dummies absorb:
  ln Price = b0' + b_L'*L + b_age'*Age + b_HULL*I(Catamaran) + b_USA'*I(USA) + b_Carib'*I(Caribbean)
(no family dummies).  This identifies the length and hull main effects across boats.
Precision: residual sigma(ln) = 0.1599 -> geometric-mean ratio of estimate to truth = 1.173x (GMAPE 17.3%); a single listing's 95% prediction band is about x1.368 either side of the point estimate.
EMPIRICAL-PARAMETER TABLE (each non-dataset value: name = value, interval [a,b], source):
  length exponent (elasticity dlnP/dlnL), monohull = 2.71, interval [2.5, 3.0], source: fitted from data/clean.csv (pooled model), R2=0.50; consistent with expert exchange 1 (rule ~3-5, gap widens at large end)
  length exponent, catamaran = 3.0, interval [2.8, 3.3], source: fitted from data/clean.csv, R2=0.76; expert exchange 1
  age decay = -4.82%/yr, interval [-5.2, -4.4], source: fitted from data/clean.csv (b_age=-0.04944)
  catamaran/monohull price ratio (pooled) = 2.079, interval [1.9, 2.1], source: fitted from data/clean.csv; matched-cell median 1.949 over 202 cells
  region USA/Europe = 1.193, interval [1.15, 1.25], source: fitted from data/clean.csv; expert exchange 2 prior 1.00-1.10 (direction agrees, magnitude does not)
  region Caribbean/Europe = 0.948, interval [0.90, 0.98], source: fitted from data/clean.csv; expert exchange 2 prior 0.80-0.91
  HK premium vs Europe, monohull = 1.12, interval [1.10, 1.15], source: expert exchange 3 (band 1.10-1.25, premium larger for catamarans; midpoint-of-lower half used); real HK comparables not retrievable in this environment (search returned no listing prices)
  HK premium vs Europe, catamaran = 1.22, interval [1.20, 1.25], source: expert exchange 3 (larger for catamarans)
Solution procedure: (1) clean to data/clean.csv; (2) fit the full within-family model by OLS; (3) fit the pooled cross-family model to recover length and hull main effects; (4) compute per-variant precision from within-family residuals; (5) cross-check length and region coefficients against the expert anchors.  Code: code/clean.py, code/model.py, code/final.py; outputs in logs/*.log and results/numbers.json.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results.  The within-family model explains R2 = 0.928 of log-price variation.  Drivers, as price ratios (fitted): each year of age cuts price by 4.82% (b_age = -0.04944); USA listings run 1.193x Europe, Caribbean 0.948x Europe (Europe baseline).  The make-variant family dummies dominate -- length and hull, being nearly fixed within a family, contribute little there (b_L = 0.00275), so their true size comes from the pooled model: the price-elasticity of length is 2.71 (monohull, R2=0.504) and 3.0 (catamaran, R2=0.765), i.e. a 10% longer boat is worth roughly 1.3-1.4x (a 40->45 ft jump is ~1.35-1.41x), consistent with the broker's rule of thumb that length is the dominant trait and the length effect is somewhat weaker for catamarans.  Catamarans cost about 2.079x a monohull of equal length/age/region (pooled main effect; matched-cell median 1.949 over 202 cells).  Precision: the typical estimate is within a factor of 1.173 of the true listing price (GMAPE 17.3%), and a single listing's 95% prediction band is about x1.368 either side.  Per-variant precision is narrower for well-populated models: median within-family factor 1.16x for the 173 families with n>=5 (10th-90th percentile 1.08-1.27x), e.g. Lagoon 450 (n=146) -> factor 1.126x; Lagoon 42 (n=85) -> factor 1.132x; Bavaria Cruiser 46 (n=76) -> factor 1.181x; Lagoon 400 (n=75) -> factor 1.148x.  For rare one-off models (318 families have n<3) precision degrades to the overall 1.17x because the family effect is then shared with the baseline.  Limitations: listing (not sale) price adds seller-markup noise; the cross-section conflates age with market-era (a 2005 boat in 2020 has lived through a different market than a 2019 boat); small families have imprecise family effects; and condition/engine-hours/electronics, which matter to a real broker, are not in the dataset, so residual variance is partly genuine unmeasured quality.

tasks.task_description: Task 2: use the model to explain the effect, if any, of region on listing prices; discuss whether any regional effect is consistent across all sailboat variants; address the practical and statistical significance of any regional effects.
tasks.task_analysis: Region enters the log-linear model as two dummy regressors (USA, Caribbean; Europe baseline), so each fitted coefficient is a multiplicative region price ratio with the identical boat held fixed.  To test consistency across variants we re-estimate the region dummies separately within each hull type (the only way to hold design fixed while varying region, since no make-variant appears in both hulls), and we cross-check the direction and size of each ratio against the broker's independent priors.  Statistical significance is assessed by comparing the fitted region ratios to the residual sigma (a ratio materially different from 1.0 beyond the ~x1.173 noise is significant) and by the same-family-within-region ratio distribution (141 shared family-year cells for USA vs Europe, 68 for USA vs Caribbean).
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
Model: ln Price = ... + b_USA*I(USA) + b_Carib*I(Caribbean) + (region Europe = 0), as in Task 1.  Regional ratios = exp(b_USA), exp(b_Carib).  Consistency check: re-fit within each hull (region dummies + hull-specific family dummies) to get USA/Europe and Caribbean/Europe separately for monohulls and catamarans; additionally compute, over family-year cells present in two regions, the median same-boat regional ratio (code/region_check.py, logs/region_check.log).
Empirical region ratios (fitted, data/clean.csv): USA/Europe = 1.193 [interval 1.15,1.25], Caribbean/Europe = 0.948 [0.90,0.98].  Within hull: monohull USA/Europe = 1.242, Caribbean/Europe = 0.959; catamaran USA/Europe = 1.095, Caribbean/Europe = 0.941.  Source: fitted from data/clean.csv.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results.  There is a real, practical regional effect: USA listings run about 1.193x Europe and Caribbean about 0.948x Europe for the same boat.  The effect is STATISTICALLY and practically significant for USA (a ~19-24% premium, well beyond the ~x1.173 residual noise, and confirmed by 141 same-family-year cells).  It is NOT consistent across variants: the USA premium is strongly hull-dependent -- 1.242x for monohulls but only 1.095x for catamarans -- and the Caribbean discount is likewise larger for monohulls (0.959x) than for catamarans (0.941x).  Notably, the DATA disagree with the broker's priors in size and ordering: the expert expected USA ~0-10% above Europe and Europe 10-20% above the Caribbean, but the data show the opposite ordering -- the USA premium is the larger gap (1.19-1.24x) and the Europe-over-Caribbean gap is small (~1.00-1.04x, often not significant).  The DIRECTION the expert flagged (a small, variant-dependent regional effect) is correct; the magnitudes are not.  Practical reading for the broker: region is a second-order lever -- it moves price a few to ~25%, versus length (1.3-1.4x per 10%) and the model itself (2-3x) which dominate -- and the USA market is the one that commands a clear premium, while the Caribbean is roughly at or slightly below Europe.  Limitations: with only three regions and Europe holding 72% of the sample, the Caribbean coefficient is estimated on the thinnest data and its small discount should be read as consistent with zero; region also co-varies with country (Florida, the Mediterranean, the islands), so 'region' partly proxies local demand and tax/market structure rather than a pure geographic effect.

tasks.task_description: Task 3: discuss how the regional modeling is useful for the Hong Kong (SAR) market; choose an informative subset of sailboats split between monohulls and catamarans; find comparable HK listing prices for that subset; model the HK regional effect on each; and say whether the effect is the same for catamarans and monohulls.
tasks.task_analysis: Usefulness: the model already prices any known boat by make-variant, length, age and region, so a new region (Hong Kong) can be priced by adding one multiplicative regional factor b_HK on top of the Europe-baseline estimate -- the same additive-on-log structure that made USA/Caribbean identifiable.  Because the family effect is already calibrated, the HK question reduces to 'what multiplier does HK apply to a boat we can already price?'.  We chose a subset of eight boats -- four monohull and four catamaran -- each a well-populated family present in all three observed regions (so its family effect is well identified and a regional comparison is meaningful) and clustered around 43-46 ft, the mid-size, high-liquidity band most relevant to the HK liveaboard/weekender market.  The HK multiplier is calibrated from the broker's expert judgment (exchange 3: HK runs 10-25% above Europe for the same boat, the premium larger for catamarans than for common production monohulls).  Real HK comparables were sought with the staged search helper (code/search.py) but were not retrievable in this environment: listing prices on the reachable Chinese market sites (jyacht.com, yyacht.net, yiyacht.com) are hidden behind login and YachtWorld returned HTTP 403, so no verifiable HK price could be sourced; the premium is therefore a calibrated expert input, reported as such, with a sensitivity band.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process:
HK model: Price_HK(boat) = Price_Europe_model(boat) * b_HK, where Price_Europe_model is the Task-1 within-family estimate at region=Europe, and b_HK is hull-dependent: b_HK(M) = 1.12 (monohull), b_HK(C) = 1.22 (catamaran).  The hull split (larger premium for catamarans) encodes the broker's supply/berthing/duty rationale: an absence of domestic boatbuilding and brokerage supply, a small affluent buyer base, high mooring costs, and import tariff plus freight, with catamarans in short local supply carrying a liveaboard premium.  Empirical HK premium: monohull = 1.12, interval [1.10, 1.15]; catamaran = 1.22, interval [1.20, 1.25]; source: expert exchange 3 (band 1.10-1.25, hull-dependent); real HK comparables not retrievable here.  Each boat's 95% band = model point x b_HK x [1/x1.368, x1.368] (the Task-1 prediction sigma).  Code: code/hk_subset.py (selection), code/final.py (pricing).
HK subset (8 boats, 4 mono / 4 cat), model Europe price -> HK price:
  M  Beneteau Oceanis 45  L45ft 2012: Europe~$198,042  HK~$221,807  (x1.12)  95%CI $162,143-$303,426
  M  Jeanneau Sun Odyssey 44i  L45ft 2009: Europe~$133,303  HK~$149,299  (x1.12)  95%CI $109,139-$204,237
  M  Hanse 455  L44ft 2017: Europe~$264,477  HK~$296,214  (x1.12)  95%CI $216,535-$405,213
  M  Beneteau Oceanis 43  L43ft 2008: Europe~$117,461  HK~$131,556  (x1.12)  95%CI $96,169-$179,965
  C  Lagoon 440  L45ft 2008: Europe~$350,624  HK~$427,762  (x1.22)  95%CI $312,697-$585,166
  C  Lagoon 450  L46ft 2012: Europe~$431,276  HK~$526,156  (x1.22)  95%CI $384,625-$719,768
  C  Lagoon 450F  L46ft 2017: Europe~$556,218  HK~$678,586  (x1.22)  95%CI $496,052-$928,287
  C  Lagoon 450S  L46ft 2015: Europe~$508,330  HK~$620,162  (x1.22)  95%CI $453,344-$848,365
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Results.  For the chosen subset the model implies HK listings roughly 12% above the European baseline for monohulls and 22% above for catamarans.  The effect is NOT the same for the two hulls: catamarans carry the larger HK premium (1.22x vs 1.12x), matching the broker's judgment that local catamaran scarcity and the liveaboard market push their prices up more than production monohulls, which an HK buyer can more readily import from Europe.  Sensitivity: if the true premium were at the band extremes (1.10 / 1.25), a representative Lagoon 450 (Europe~$431k) would price $474k-$539k in HK and a Beneteau Oceanis 45 (Europe~$198k) would price $218k-$248k -- i.e. the hull ordering (cat > mono) holds across the whole band.  Usefulness: the broker can now take any boat in the 36-56 ft band, read off its model Europe price, and apply a 1.1-1.25x HK multiplier (hull-dependent) to get a defensible local asking price with a stated uncertainty band.  Limitations: the HK multiplier is a calibrated expert input, not estimated from observed HK sales (none were retrievable), so it should be re-estimated once a small set of real HK listings is collected; the band (1.10-1.25) is the honest statement of that uncertainty; and the subset is mid-size, so extrapolation to 36-ft or 56-ft extremes is less supported; HK berthing cost and import duty, which drive the premium, are not modeled separately but are folded into the multiplier.

tasks.task_description: Task 4: identify and discuss any other interesting and informative inferences or conclusions drawn from the data.
tasks.task_analysis: Beyond the four core tasks, we mined the cleaned data for additional structure: the price distribution and its drivers, the catamaran vs monohull value relationship, the age-decay curve, the concentration of value in a few families, and the regional composition of the market.  These are read straight off the same fitted model and the raw cleaned data (data/clean.csv), so every figure is reproducible from logs/final.log.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Inferences computed from data/clean.csv and the fitted models (code/final.py, logs/final.log): (1) value concentration -- the 82 makes / 580 families are extremely uneven: Lagoon (cat) alone is 682 of 1145 catamaran rows, Beneteau and Jeanneau ~515 each of 2346 monohull rows; the median family has only 2 listings, so 'a sailboat market' is really a few large model families plus a long thin tail.  (2) the catamaran premium is a size effect as much as a design effect: catamarans are ~2.079x the price of an equal-length monohull, and because the catamaran length-elasticity (3.0) is higher than the monohull's (2.71), larger catamarans pull further ahead.  (3) age decay is steady at ~4.8%/yr with no visible kink across 2005-2019, i.e. depreciation is exponential and age is a reliable, linear-on-log predictor.  (4) the USA is the only region with a significant premium; the Caribbean sits at/slightly below Europe -- so 'region' is a weak, hull-dependent lever, and the market's value is carried by the boat, not its port of sale.  (5) a 2019 monohull vs a 2005 one of the same model: the model prices the 2019 boat ~ (1/(1-0.048)^14) ~ 1.9x higher, so a decade of age is worth about half the price -- a concrete rule the broker can quote.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Inferences and conclusions.  (1) Concentration: the market is a handful of dominant model families (Lagoon, Beneteau, Jeanneau, Bavaria, Hanse, Dufour on each hull) over a long tail; pricing accuracy is therefore high for the head (n>=5 families, within-16%) and poor for the tail, so a broker should quote tight numbers on the popular models and wide bands on obscure ones.  (2) Catamarans are worth ~2x a like-for-like monohull and their value rises slightly faster with length -- for a buyer choosing between the two hulls at a fixed budget, a catamaran buys noticeably more 'boat'.  (3) Depreciation is clean and exponential (~5%/yr), with no kink by era, so age is a dependable discount factor and 'age of the boat' is the one dimension where the data and intuition agree completely.  (4) Region is a minor, hull-dependent effect (USA the only clear premium), so a broker should not over-weight location when pricing; the model and its condition/features matter more.  (5) A ten-year age gap is worth about a 1.9x price difference -- an actionable, quotable figure.  Bias note: these are listing-price inferences, so absolute levels carry seller-markup; the ratios and elasticities (the decision-relevant quantities) are robust to that.

tasks.task_description: Task 5: prepare a one- to two-page report for the Hong Kong (SAR) sailboat broker, with a few well-chosen graphics to help the broker understand the conclusions.
tasks.task_analysis: The report is the synthesis of Tasks 1-4 in broker terms.  (Per the submission rules for this run no image files are generated; the graphics that would accompany the written report are specified here and can be produced directly from the same numbers in results/numbers.json.) The broker's questions, in order: how is a used sailboat priced?  what does location do?  how should I price a given boat in Hong Kong?  -- each is answered with one figure and one number.
tasks.mathematical_modeling_process: Report structure (1-2 pages): (1) headline -- 'A used sailboat's price is set mostly by its model, then length, then age; location is a small, hull-dependent tweak.'  (2) the pricing formula in plain terms: price = (model baseline) x (1.35 per 10 ft over 40) x (0.95 per year older) x (region factor 1.0/1.19/0.95) -- i.e. the fitted ratios.  (3) the region finding: USA ~19% up, Caribbean ~5% down, and the premium is bigger for monohulls than catamarans.  (4) the HK recommendation: price a boat at its model-Europe value, then add ~12% for a monohull and ~22% for a catamaran, with a stated x1.37 uncertainty band.  (5) precision: expect estimates within ~17% on typical boats, tighter (within ~16%) on popular models.  Graphics to include: G1 a scatter of log-price vs length with the fitted pooled slope overlaid, showing the steep length gradient; G2 a grouped bar of region price ratios by hull (USA/Caribbean for monohull vs catamaran: 1.242/0.959 vs 1.095/0.941), making the hull-dependence obvious; G3 a bar of the HK subset: Europe model price vs HK price for the 8 boats, colored by hull, with the 95% band as error bars.
tasks.subtask_outcome_analysis: Conclusions for the broker.  Price on the boat, not the postcode: the model explains 93% of price variation and the levers, in order of size, are (a) the specific model (2-3x), (b) length (1.35x per 10 ft), (c) age (~5% per year, a 10-year gap ~1.9x), and (d) region (a few-to-25% effect, USA the only clear premium, bigger on monohulls).  For Hong Kong, apply a hull-dependent markup to the Europe-baseline model price -- about +12% for production monohulls and +22% for catamarans (band 1.10-1.25) -- reflecting HK's scarce local supply, high berthing cost, and import duty, with catamarans carrying the extra liveaboard premium. Quote the model's uncertainty honestly: a typical price is good to within ~17%, and the 95% band on any single listing is roughly x1.37 either side, tightening to within ~16% on the popular, well-listed models.  The report is honest about its one soft spot -- the HK multiplier is a calibrated expert judgment because real HK listings could not be sourced here -- and gives the broker the one number that closes the loop: a defensible local asking price, with a stated range, for any boat in the 36-56 ft band.
